title: Photography direction for a logistics company
metaTitle: Logistics photography that shows the work
excerpt: Photograph the freight, the equipment, and the document that closes the job. A globe or a stock container reassures the team and tells an operator you have nothing of yours to show.
alt: A hand pinning string between printed mobile screens on a wall, planning a sequence the way a photo brief should plan what the frame must prove.
caption: A hand pinning string between printed mobile screens. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should logistics photography show?
faqs.answer: Show the work an operator can check: the equipment you run, a load you are allowed to photograph, or a document such as a POD with private fields covered. Put that frame next to a sentence about the move. A container on the water, a globe, or a skyline does not answer whether you can make their appointment.

faqs.question: How do we brief a shoot for a carrier site?
faqs.answer: List five frames before the day: equipment, a real or clearly labeled load, the closing document, the place you serve if place matters, and a portrait only with permission. Include the mode words the site already uses, and shoot a center-weighted crop for a phone. Reject any frame you cannot caption with a fact.

faqs.question: What if we cannot photograph customer freight?
faqs.answer: Use type, a labeled sample, or your own yard and equipment. Say when a number or a document is a sample. Do not rent a stock container to fill the gap. A plain sentence about mode, region, and cutoff is more credible than a picture of someone else's ship.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Good logistics company website photography shows the work, not a globe. A stock photo of a shipping container is the picture teams reach for because it looks like the industry. An operator who needs to know you can move the thing has seen that frame on every competitor and every bank ad. It argues that you have nothing of yours to show.

The pictures are part of the argument. They should be able to sit next to a sentence about a cutoff, a seal, or a POD and not embarrass the sentence.

## A photograph is a claim about a load

Every frame claims "this is what it is like to ship with us." A container on open water claims you are a mood about trade. A handshake in a clean vest claims the work is a meeting. A drone shot of a port claims scale you may not operate. None of those claims help a coordinator decide whether you can make a Tuesday appointment.

Nielsen Norman Group's research on visits is the time box. People often leave in the first 10 to 20 seconds, and the value has to be visible within about 10 if you want them to stay. On a phone that window is one picture and a few lines. If the picture is a globe, the lines have to fight it. They usually lose, and the operator leaves with the costume instead of the move.

Brief the frame the way you brief a dispatcher. What freight. What equipment. What fact a peer would check. What must not appear because it is a different mode or a different promise. A mood board of blue and orange is not a brief. It postpones the claim.

The W3C's accessibility principles start with perceivable. A fact that exists only inside a photograph, with no sentence beside it, is easy to miss and unavailable to someone who cannot see the picture. Let the photo carry the yard, the trailer, the dock. Put the cities, the clock, and the refusal in text. Alt text should describe the picture, not the slogan you hoped it proved.

## What the work looks like

A usable frame contains evidence. A trailer number and a seal you are allowed to show. A pallet count at a dock. A reefer unit if you haul cold freight. A liftgate on the truck you actually send to sites without a dock. A POD with private fields covered, if the document is the proof. Ordinary and specific beats dramatic and generic.

Show people doing the job when you have permission. A dispatcher on a real board. A driver checking securement on freight that matches your mode. Faces are optional. The task is not. If someone is identifiable, they have agreed, and the caption can name the role without inventing a story about their passion.

Skip the fake UI floating over a highway. If you show a screen, show a status a shipper would recognize, and label it as a sample when the numbers are not from a live load. A card that says "delivered" with no reference, no time, and no place is an advertisement. The operator can tell.

One frame at the top of the homepage is enough. A carousel of ports, planes, and trucks says you do everything, which is the globe in motion. Pick the move you want to be hired for this quarter. Change the picture when that work changes. Do not rotate audiences and call it relevance.

## Reject the container

Put the stock container on a kill list, in writing, before the shoot and before the stock search.

Also reject: a globe or a network of dots. An unmarked vessel. A skyline. Two people pointing at a laptop with an unreadable map. A pallet of anonymous boxes in a warehouse that could be a furniture brand. A high-visibility vest with no freight in the frame. Any picture you cannot caption with equipment, a document, or a place you serve.

Reject art that hides a second call to action. A phone mockup with two equal buttons, a billboard inside the photo, a "track / quote" split rendered as a poster. The page already has a quote path. The picture should not invent a second decision, and it should not split the one you have.

If a collaborator adds the container back "so it feels like logistics," the kill list is the reply. Logistics, for your buyer, feels like a load that moved. Warmth is welcome when it is the light on your dock. A rented coastline is not warmth. It is a category error.

## Direct a small shoot

Decide five frames before the day, and stop there.

The equipment you run, close enough to identify. A load in progress that you are allowed to photograph, or a clearly labeled sample. The document that closes the job, cropped to the fact and stripped of private data. The place that matters, if a terminal or a region is the offer, shot so a local operator might recognize the kind of building. A portrait of the person who answers exceptions, only with permission, and only if the about page names them.

Give the photographer the vocabulary from the services page. If the word is "dry van" and not "global network," the trailer should be a dry van. Props from another mode will be read as a promise. A shipping container on a site that does not book ocean freight is not a metaphor. It is a lead you will have to decline.

Screens need a pass before the shutter. Real customer names and addresses in a mock are a privacy problem. Obvious nonsense is a credibility problem. Use sample labels, and use the columns a coordinator expects.

Shoot for the phone crop. A wide yard that only works as a desktop hero will be cut until the trailer is gone and the sky remains. Put the evidence near the center. The phone is the primary frame for someone standing on a dock.

## Sequence and caption

Place the work picture next to the sentence that states the move. Do not lead with a mood and bury the dock three sections down. People who leave in the first seconds leave with whatever you put there.

Caption the fact. "Appointment delivery, dock to dock, POD the same afternoon." Not a joke, and not a keyword. Alt text describes what is visible: the trailer, the dock, the document. If the picture is licensed, the credit can live in the caption. The caption still has to say what the frame is for.

Do not set a headline across the only evidence. Type over a seal, a piece count, or a face removes the proof and keeps the decoration. If type must sit on the image, put it in the empty sky or the empty floor, and leave the work readable.

Motion usually delays the claim. A slow pan across a port, a looping globe, a video that must play before the quote button is stable. Ship the still. If something moves, it should reveal the evidence, and it should respect a reduced-motion setting. A clear still beats a sequence that is almost clear.

## When a photograph is the wrong tool

Some proofs are clearer as type or as a marked-up document. A detention rule. A list of states. A cutoff. Forcing those into a lifestyle frame produces a confused scene and a caption that does the real work. Use the sentence. A quiet page is allowed to be mostly words. Words are how the boundary stays exact.

Illustration is honest when you cannot show the freight or the customer. Label it as a diagram or a sample. A specific lane, a specific piece count, and a specific refusal can be drawn. A globe with a glowing arc cannot, not for this job. That drawing is the stock container in another medium.

Buy fewer pictures. Three accurate frames and a lot of plain background will feel more serious than a unique photograph in every section, half of them arguing with the copy. The sections that explain accessorials can be type. They do not need a ship.

## A kill list you keep in the file

Write the rejected frames where the next person will see them: in the photo brief and at the top of the design file. Container on water. Globe. Unmarked port. Vest with no freight. Laptop with an unreadable map. Two equal buttons inside the art. If a frame is added later, it has to survive that list and a one-line caption a dispatcher would accept.

Review the live homepage after the pictures are in, not only the contact sheet. A beautiful dock photo that pushes the quote below a fold, or that has type across the seal, has failed in the layout even if the shoot was right. Crop again or move the type. The argument is the move plus the door. The picture serves that, or it leaves.

Replace a frame when the mode changes. A reefer story illustrated with a dry van is the same error as the container, just more local. The library can keep the old picture for the old page. The current page shows the current work.

The frame that works on a wide monitor often fails in the first phone screen, where the crop and the quote path share a few hundred pixels. That visit is [the mobile visit for a logistics company](/blog/the-mobile-visit-for-a-logistics-company).

For a look at how a public site can show finished work without a costume, see [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works).
